history.recommendation_text: The Board reiterated its recommendation that the Administration expand the donor base to encourage contributions, on a voluntary basis, to the capitalization of the Joint Sustainable Development Goals Fund at the required levels.
history.administration_response: The annual contribution to the Joint Sustainable Development Goals Fund increased from $42.9 million in 2020 to $79.2 million in 2021. The Fund also attracted a new donor to join as a contributor. That said, the Fund’s capitalization is well below the level of $290 million per annum requested of Member States in the quadrennial comprehensive policy review funding compact. The Fund has initiated donor assessments (November 2021) and a number of retreats with its governance partners (Operational Steering Committee: November 2021) and stakeholder groups (February 2022) to advocate additional funding. It has also initiated discussions on launching thematic windows (during its development partners retreat in February 2022) and activated a development emergency modality (activated for COVID-19 on July 2021). Discussions are currently under way (March 2022) regarding the possible activation of the development emergency modality.
history.board_assessment: Given that the Development Coordination Office has made progress in broadening the donor base and increasing annual contributions, although the resources mobilized are far from target amount, the Board considers this recommendation to be under implementation.

history.recommendation_text: The Board reiterated its recommendation that the Administration expand the donor base to encourage contributions, on a voluntary basis, to the capitalization of the Joint Sustainable Development Goals Fund at the required levels.
history.administration_response: As of December 2022, the Joint Sustainable Development Goals Fund had received a total of $254 million from 14 donor partners, 13 of which were Member States. The top four donors – Sweden, Spain, the European Union and the Kingdom of the Netherlands – accounted for more than 80 per cent of the total contributions to the Fund. However, this level of mobilization is well below the target of $290 million a year pledged to the Fund by Member States as part of their funding compact in support of United Nations development system reform. Recognizing the difficulties in the development aid landscape, the Fund is exploring new opportunities in partnership with United Nations entities to tap into thematic resources by incubating and launching dedicated thematic windows related to key Sustainable Development Goal transformations. This strategic move aligns with the future vision of the Fund to become the flagship financing mechanism for United Nations collective action on key Sustainable Development Goals, as well as respond to the recommendations of the system-wide evaluation. Based on this approach, there have been promising discussions with donors, including the European Union, Germany, Spain, Belgium, Denmark and others, in relation to the Fund or a particular thematic window.
history.board_assessment: Given that the Development Coordination Office is exploring new opportunities in broadening the donor base and increasing annual contributions, but the resources mobilized are far below the target, the Board considers this recommendation to be under implementation.

history.sg_progress: The Joint Sustainable Development Goals Fund has undergone significant governance reforms in response to the system-wide evaluation, resulting in the Development Coordination Office formally becoming the Chair of the operational steering committee. In addition, the strategic advisory group, chaired by the Deputy Secretary-General, has been reformed to foster stronger engagement with Member States. In alignment with the United Nations Sustainable Development Group key transitions, the Fund has developed a new multi-year strategy, which will be endorsed at the upcoming meeting of the strategic advisory group. Notably, the Fund’s prominence was recognized by Member States during the operational activities for development segment of the Economic and Social Council in May 2023. It featured in Council resolution 2023/31, the Secretary-General’s report on progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals (A/78/80-E/2023/64) and the draft political declaration of Member States for the Sustainable Development Goals Summit. The Deputy Secretary-General launched the Fund’s food systems window during the Food Systems Summit stocktaking held in Rome in July 2023 and the Assistant Secretary-General for Development Coordination advocated for the Fund during the high-level political forum on sustainable development, under the auspices of the Economic and Social Council, in July 2023. The secretariat of the Joint Sustainable Development Goals Fund, under the leadership of the Development Coordination Office and its operational steering committee, remains committed to reinforcing resource mobilization efforts in collaboration with Member States and other partners to bridge the gap and reach the funding target.

history.recommendation_text: The Board reiterated its recommendation that the Administration expand the donor base to encourage contributions, on a voluntary basis, to the capitalization of the Joint Sustainable Development Goals Fund at the required levels.
history.administration_response: Capitalization of the Joint Sustainable Development Goals Fund saw a notable increase in 2023 compared to 2022, as the Fund received $55.9 million in total contributions along with securing $58.8 million in signed commitments for 2024. The Joint Sustainable Development Goals Fund also expanded its donor base from 13 to 16 donors with Belgium, Italy and Saudi Arabia joining as new contribution partners. This positive momentum signifies buy-in from the Joint Sustainable Development Goals Fund’s contributing partners on the Fund’s new strategic approach that is aligned with propelling the transitions, especially for thematic areas that are in line with the donor Governments’ national priorities for development assistance. The heightened role of the Joint Sustainable Development Goals Fund and the resident coordinator system, along with the imperative for their full capitalization, has been championed by the Secretary-General and United Nations leadership and has been prominently featured in diverse United Nations forums and conferences. That elevated push is underscored by the resolution adopted by the Economic and Social Council during its 2023 operational activities for development segment, the Secretary-General’s call for increased capitalization for the Fund in his report on progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals to the high-level political forum on sustainable development in 2023 and culminating in the political declaration of the Sustainable Development Goals Summit in 2023. Recognizing the need for further capitalization, the Fund, under the guidance of the Operational Steering Committee, plans to launch a new resource mobilization strategy by the second quarter of 2024, focused on expanding the donor base, also encouraging programme country contributions, and advocating for the importance of unearmarked, multi-year commitments to global pooled funds in general to ensure the flexibility, predictability and high quality of financing for the Joint Sustainable Development Goals Fund.
history.board_assessment: Given that a new resource mobilization strategy that focuses on expanding the donor base is planned to be launched by the second quarter of 2024, the Board considers this recommendation to be under implementation.

history.sg_progress: As of August 2024, the Joint Sustainable Development Goals Fund had already seen a 10 per cent increase in resource mobilization, receiving $61.5 million in commitments in 2024, compared with $55.9 million overall in 2023. This indicates continued support for the Fund’s new strategy, which is focused on propelling key Goal transitions. The capitalization of the Fund is also featured prominently in the new funding compact as the United Nations premier innovative funding mechanism to accelerate the achievement of the Goals. Cognizant that the Fund requires continued and scaled-up support from Member States and other donors to reach its required level of capitalization to promote transformative change for Goal transitions by 2030, the Administration requests the closure of this recommendation, given that efforts to expand the donor base have already resulted in an increase in donor commitments.

history.recommendation_text: The Board reiterated its recommendation that the Administration expand the donor base to encourage contributions, on a voluntary basis, to the capitalization of the Joint Sustainable Development Goals Fund at the required levels.
history.administration_response: The Joint Sustainable Development Goals Fund achieved strong growth in capitalization during 2024, reaching $89.9 million in deposits received, which represents a substantial (160 per cent) increase from 2023 levels. This significant growth demonstrates increasing donor confidence in the Fund’s innovative strategy, which is centred on key Sustainable Development Goal transitions, and the strategy’s vital role in implementing the Pact for the Future. Considering the current undercapitalization compared with the annual goal of $500 million under the funding compact, the Fund, together with the Peacebuilding Fund and the Central Emergency Response Fund, is developing a joint resource mobilization strategy to enhance synergies and appeal to a broader donor base. While the Development Coordination Office takes the lead on resource mobilization efforts, it is important to note that the Joint Sustainable Development Goals Fund is an inter-agency mechanism that requires active commitment from its United Nations entity partners and Member States to achieve full capitalization.
history.board_assessment: Given that the Fund is developing a joint resource mobilization strategy to enhance synergies and appeal to a broader donor base, the Board considers the recommendation to be under implementation.

history.recommendation_text: In paragraph 516 of its report, the Board reiterated its recommendation that the Administration expand the donor base to encourage contributions, on a voluntary basis, to the capitalization of the Joint Sustainable Development Goals Fund at the required levels.
history.reference_raw: Report of the Board for the year ended 31 December 2020 6
history.sg_progress: As of June 2025, the Joint Sustainable Development Goals Fund had received approximately $40 million in deposits and signed contributions, with a realistic projection of $50 to $55 million by year-end. This anticipated capitalization follows the Fund’s growth trajectory, which saw $89.7 million in contributions in 2024. At the July 2025 meeting of the Strategic Advisory Group, chaired by the Deputy Secretary-General, Member States expressed a strong consensus on positioning the Fund as the leading platform for implementation of the outcomes of the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development. Participants committed to intensifying advocacy and resource mobilization efforts. In line with the decision taken by the Executive Committee established by the Secretary-General, the Fund has developed a joint resource mobilization strategy in collaboration with the Central Emergency Response Fund and the Peacebuilding Fund, which has been endorsed by the Executive Office of the Secretary-General. The strategy aims to enhance synergies and broaden donor engagement. The Joint Sustainable Development Goals Fund has also received encouraging signals regarding additional commitments from the Global Flagship Initiative for Food Security, which supports food systems programming in various developing countries, highlighting the Fund’s efforts to diversify and strengthen financing for key transitions. One Member State has reaffirmed its leadership as the Fund’s largest supporter, pledging an additional 28 million euros in unearmarked contributions for the period 2025–2026 and another 4 million euros earmarked for Sustainable Development Goal localization until 2028. Another Member State has emerged as a strategic partner, providing earmarked support for food systems and for programming relating to the Global Accelerator on Jobs and Social Protection for Just Transitions, reflecting growing engagement. Despite these positive developments, donor concentration remains a concern, underscoring the urgent need for diversification. Strategic Advisory Group members have committed to pursuing multi-year pledges, prioritizing unearmarked contributions and leveraging global platforms to highlight the Fund’s alignment with the reform objectives of the UN80 Initiative and its role in reducing system fragmentation. However, current capitalization levels remain significantly below the funding compact target of $500 million annually, emphasizing the continued need for expanded donor engagement and enhanced resource mobilization to fully realize the Fund’s potential by 2030.
